status: Research only; production source, installed Go, module cache, driver and system network settings remain unchanged.

environments.primary: Windows native sender 192.0.2.10 to Linux Chrome 192.0.2.20 over the physical Wi-Fi LAN; direct IPv4 UDP, no TURN.
environments.reverse: Linux native sender 192.0.2.20 to Windows Chrome 192.0.2.10 over the same physical LAN; changes both endpoint roles and receiver OS/browser, so it does not isolate the sender alone.
environments.sameHost: Windows native sender to Windows Chrome through the host LAN address; routes locally without the physical Wi-Fi hop. This is not a LAN throughput claim.
environments.windowsNIC: Realtek 8852CE WiFi 6E PCI-E NIC; reported link speed 2.4 Gbps; driver 6001.16.172.0 dated 2025-10-16. Reported link speed is not available application bandwidth.

method.connection: Exactly one PeerConnection, one reliable ordered DataChannel, one SCTP association and one native UniversalUDPMux socket per trial.
method.emptyVideo: A recvonly video transceiver is present in every arm, including all baselines.
method.crypto: Production sealed-record construction and browser authentication/decryption, with four decoder operations; final plaintext and ciphertext SHA-256 equality checked for every successful transfer.
method.timing: Browser start request to last authenticated plaintext; includes transfer slow start. Excludes sender file reading/sealing, ICE/DTLS setup, final whole-file hashes and disk output. Cached input and memory output are not the full product pipeline.
method.repetition: Most parameter arms are single screening runs. The confirm batch alternates baseline and overlapped submission across three 473 MB transfers per arm. local-long repeats the ordinary baseline three times. reverse-repeat runs three 473 MB transfers for each of three arms, reversing order for the middle repetition. No warmups were excluded from these batches.
method.TCP: 64 MiB raw TCP transfer with receiver byte count and SHA-256 before/after primary batches and reverse-repeat. Reverse-repeat uses a connection initiated by Windows with Linux sending the data; an earlier inbound Windows listening control timed out. No firewall settings changed. TCP is a path-capacity control, not an equivalent application/crypto benchmark.
method.timingCounters: Native counters are wall time spent inside calls, not CPU time. Sampled intervals subtract the first sample from the last to reduce startup effects. Kernel/driver waits, scheduling and packet processing are not separated by these counters.
method.dropCounters: Linux /proc/net/snmp deltas are host-wide observations, not definitive per-flow attribution. They are unavailable for the Windows receiver controls.
method.source: Local research harness and raw reports remain in .tmp/webrtc-single-20261022. All dependency experiments use local copies or Go build overlays.
method.changes: Screened send-watermarks, pacing/burst sizes, SCTP congestion growth, MTU, socket buffers, context cancellation, DTLS batching, Windows UDP segmentation, bounded overlapped send submission, connected UDP, and Linux sendmmsg batching.

interpretations: A 20 MB/s universal SCTP/WebRTC single-connection limit is contradicted by the local single-connection control. A same-host result does not establish physical LAN or WAN performance.

The primary Windows-to-Linux direction often spends most of the native send loop in UDP write calls despite sufficiently large congestion/receive windows and sometimes zero observed receiver drops. This localizes work but does not prove a specific kernel, driver, filter or CPU cause.
Reducing approximately 100,000 UDP send calls to roughly 6,000 with Windows segmentation did not establish a repeatable doubling. Fewer syscalls alone are insufficient on this path.
Reverse-direction queue-depth gains are environment dependent; use actual progress and byte ownership to keep the pipeline supplied instead of adopting one large global queue.

Single-connection work and demand-driven multiple connections remain complementary. More efficient endpoints can lift a WAN ceiling; WAN RTT, loss, receive/congestion windows, path capacity and relay behavior still constrain the result.

The first Windows WSASendMsg experiments failed on immediate successful sends reported as zero bytes. A research-only Go internal/poll build overlay supplied the synchronous byte-count pointer; subsequent integrity-checked segmentation transfers succeeded. The installed Go toolchain was not modified.

The raw Windows overlapped prototype has a fixed research timeout and is not suitable for production integration without the existing cancellation/deadline owner. Connecting an ICE socket to one remote endpoint also changes filtering/recovery semantics and is diagnostic only.

largerMTUReverse473MB.interpretation: Higher individual throughput but substantial variability; do not adopt a larger global path MTU.

keyResults.conclusion: Single-connection gains are demonstrated in these small repeated samples; stable physical-LAN 40 MB/s has not been demonstrated. No universal maximum has been established.
